coursesExamined.name: Personal & Professional Development

evidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
evidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
evidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

coursesExamined.name: Research Methods & Statistics

evidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
evidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
evidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
evidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

coursesExamined.contribution: provides research design, operationalisation, sampling and statistical foundations for empirical inquiry

coursesExamined.name: Law, Society & Justice

evidence.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
evidence.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.

evidence.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. coursesExamined.name: History of Empires

evidence.description2: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
evidence.profile: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.

coursesExamined.name: Native American Histories

evidence.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
evidence.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
evidence.discipline: Indigenous studies; Social and cultural history; Public history
evidence.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
evidence.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production

coursesExamined.name: Psycholinguistics

evidence.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

descriptions.name: Writing Art's Histories
descriptions.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

comparability: The broad closest response has five specifically American historical/media courses including the current historical-research seminar, with real political institutions, literature, cultural interpretation and language study. These are substantive responses to defining target disciplines, not a generic humanities assemblage. The cultural route increases literary/media analysis and creative/documentary practice; political route adds law/rights/empire/social movements and prevention, anchored by American historical/media work. American-focused core and specific comparative methods support all three; specialist English proficiency, phonetics, World Englishes and full American literary sequences remain explicit gaps.
distinctness: Culture and interpretation replace comparative politics, international relations, peace/conflict, psycholinguistics and historical-source work with media archaeology, environmental representation, film adaptation, literary theory, creative communication, documentary and art historiography. 8 courses differ from the broad programme; this is a change of academic emphasis and method.

Political institutions, rights, law, empire, social movements and youth radicalisation replace much of the broad programme’s literature, art and language. 8 courses differ from the broad programme and 14 from the cultural programme. American-focused history/media remain the anchor; comparative law is not labelled US constitutional training.

stopping.assessment: The broad closest match is complemented by two generator-backed and feasible organising directions: American literature, media and cultural expression; and American politics, identity and global affairs. Each produces material curricular consequences and exceeds the pairwise 30-EC distinctness floor, so the maximum of three alternatives is reached. The separately evidenced English-teaching direction is not feasible because UCR does not offer a sufficiently complete sequence in English linguistics, language proficiency, second-language pedagogy and supervised teacher preparation. English as a global language is separately assessed rather than claimed as covered by psycholinguistics. The workbook supplies stylistics and neurocognitive language study, but not a sustained World Englishes, sociolinguistics, language variation or English-proficiency sequence that could support an additional complete programme.
